title: Christian Nationalism: Definition and Biblical Examination
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: Defining Christian Nationalism
subpoints: Distinguishing the term from general patriotism or cultural heritage
Using Stephen Wolfe's definition as the foundational reference
Identifying the core belief: God enters covenants with nations, granting them favored status

outline.title: Theological Implications: Theonomy and Postmillennialism
subpoints: Christian nationalism logically requires theonomy (adoption of Mosaic civil law)
Theonomy requires a postmillennial eschatological framework
The necessity of consistent theological application versus reactive rejection

outline.title: Four Distinct Forms of Christian Nationalism
subpoints: Cultural: Preserving Christian heritage in society
Political: State favoring Christian morality (aligned with Reformed confessions on government's role)
Integralist: State actively promoting Christianity and enforcing religious orthodoxy
Ethno-nationalism: Fusing Christian identity with specific ethnicity or race

outline.title: Biblical and Confessional Boundaries
subpoints: Rejecting ethno-nationalism and 'kinism' as unbiblical racial tribalism
Acknowledging the government's role to protect true worship while guarding against corruption
Avoiding both unbiblical nationalism and unbiblical secularism

summary:
In this Sunday school lesson, Pastor Tito Lyro examines the controversial concept of Christian nationalism, aiming to move beyond reactive opinions toward a careful, biblically grounded definition. He utilizes the definition provided by Stephen Wolfe, the term's originator, which posits that nations can enter into covenants with God, thereby receiving a favored status similar to that of ancient Israel. The sermon highlights that this theological framework is inextricably linked to theonomy—the belief that Mosaic civil laws should be adopted by modern governments—and postmillennialism, creating a consistent logical chain that defines the movement's core doctrine.

The lesson distinguishes four primary forms of Christian nationalism: cultural, political, integralist, and ethno-nationalist. While the political form aligns with Reformed confessional views on the state's duty to protect true worship, the integralist form advocates for the state's active promotion and enforcement of Christianity. The pastor strongly rejects ethno-nationalism and the related ideology of 'kinism,' which fuses Christian identity with racial or ethnic superiority, labeling such views as unbiblical tribalism.

Ultimately, the sermon calls for a balanced theological stance that resists both the fusion of church and state power in a corrupt political system and the secular exclusion of God from public life. By understanding the specific theological commitments required by Christian nationalism, believers are encouraged to engage with the topic through informed discernment rather than simplistic rejection or uncritical adoption.
